claims.claim: After a hundred-year war, Mahishasura takes Indra's office and the gods' jurisdictions, leaving the gods displaced.
Led by Brahma, the gods report their defeat to Shiva and Vishnu and seek a means to kill Mahishasura.
Radiances from Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma, Indra and the other gods converge as Devi.
The manuscript preserves the source-specified correspondence of divine radiances to Devi's body without adding an origin genealogy.
Shiva, Vishnu, Varuna, Agni, Vayu, Indra, Yama, Prajapati, Brahma, the Sun and Kala give Devi the listed battle equipment and powers.

claims.adaptation_note: Narrative bridge about function; it asserts no new power, origin or outcome.
claims.claim: The prose briefly explains the tactical variety of the gifts to prevent the list from reading as a contextless catalogue.
The Ocean of Milk, Vishvakarman, the Ocean, Himavat, Kubera and Shesha provide the listed adornments, armor, lion, cup and necklace.
Vishvakarman's armor is described as impenetrable, and Himavat provides Devi's lion.
Devi's roar shakes the worlds, sea, earth and mountains while gods and sages praise her.
Mahishasura approaches the roar with his army; Devi's crown, bow sound, radiance and many arms fill the worlds.
Cikshura, Chamara, Udagra, Mahahanu, Asiloman, Bashkala and Bidala lead vast contingents of chariots, elephants, cavalry and foot soldiers.

claims.adaptation_note: Editorial handling of an open Bombay-reading variant; no extra chief is introduced.
claims.claim: The narrative excludes the disputed Ugradarshana name and groups the commanders into a readable advance.
Devi cuts the enemy missiles, her lion attacks, and troops bearing varied weapons arise from her breaths.
Drums and conches accompany the breath-born troops, while Devi's weapons and bell kill, bind and confound the enemy.
The terrible battlefield is obstructed by the fallen and runs red before Devi, the lion and the breath-born troops destroy the host.

claims.adaptation_note: Violence is reduced in detail without changing the army's destruction or the field's cost.
claims.claim: Graphic details are compressed into sober consequences suitable for family reading.
The gods shower flowers after Mahishasura's host is destroyed.
Devi counters Cikshura's arrows, kills his horses and driver, breaks his bow and banner and wounds him.
Cikshura's sword breaks after striking the lion and Devi, and Devi's spear shatters his weapon and ends his attack.
Devi's utterance renders Chamara's first spear powerless and her arrows cut his next spear.
Devi's lion fights elephant-mounted Chamara to the ground and kills him with a paw-blow.
Udagra, Karala, Uddhata, Bashkala, Tamra, Andhaka, Ugrasya, Ugravirya, Mahahanu, Bidala, Durdhara and Durmukha are defeated by the source-specified means.

claims.adaptation_note: Pacing adaptation; all retained names, weapons and outcomes remain source-bound.
claims.claim: The named-chief sequence is arranged as waves of pressure rather than an unexplained roll call.
In buffalo form Mahishasura attacks the breath-born troops and Devi's lion with muzzle, hooves, tail, horns, rush, roar, circling and breath.
Mahishasura's movements disturb earth, sea, clouds and mountains.
When Devi binds Mahishasura, he shifts from buffalo to lion, armed man, elephant and buffalo again.
Devi counters the lion and armed man, cuts the elephant's trunk after it seizes her lion, and faces the returned buffalo form.

claims.adaptation_note: Causal presentation of the stated sequence, without inventing a boon or motive for the power.
claims.claim: The form changes are narrated as successive attempts to evade each counter.
Devi drinks and laughs, breaks Mahishasura's hurled mountains with arrows and warns that his roaring will be brief.
Devi leaps, pins Mahishasura's neck, strikes with the trident and beheads him while he emerges halfway from the buffalo's mouth.
The gods rejoice and celestial singers and dancers celebrate Mahishasura's death.
The gods praise Devi as cosmic power, knowledge, prosperity, protection and mercy.
The gods state in their praise that the enemies slain by Devi reach heaven and ask her forms and weapons to protect every direction.

claims.adaptation_note: Attribution safeguard required by the source-clearance contract.
claims.claim: The manuscript explicitly frames the hymn's cosmic and soteriological language as speech by the gods.
The gods worship with flowers, perfume and incense, then request relief when they remember Devi in calamity and prosperity for mortal hymn-singers.
Devi grants the stated request and disappears.
After the completed Mahishasura ending, Medhas introduces the later emergence of the Goddess from Gauri.

claims.adaptation_note: Original scene-setting and dialogue; it adds no plot fact, identity, relationship or doctrine.
claims.claim: Forest evening imagery and Medhas's opening sentence establish a quiet oral-story frame.

claims.adaptation_note: Explicitly labeled modern editorial reflection, not scripture, quotation or doctrine.
claims.claim: The labeled closing reflection observes that changing threats require attentive responses.
